title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough - batching & KV cache cost model
summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Atlas Financial through Redwood Optimize recommendations focusing on batching and prefix/KV cache strategies, presented a cost model and benchmark assumptions. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for latency-sensitive financial workflows and requested benchmark runs with their traffic patterns and security docs; agreed to pilot with cost/latency targets and follow-up SE-led benchmark session.
topics: batching strategy (dynamic batching, batch windows, throughput)
cost model and cost-per-req token math
action_items: Maya Patel: Send tailored pricing and model options by 2026-07-15
Diego Ramos: Share benchmark spreadsheet, batching config templates, and example RL client script by 2026-07-14
Rajiv Menon: Provide 7-day sample traffic profile and production request logs (anonymized) by 2026-07-18
next_steps: Schedule SE-led benchmark session week of 2026-07-20
Share SOC2 / security package link and KMS/HSM integration notes
Setup pilot agreement for Dedicated capacity if benchmarks meet latency targets
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-12 10:30 PDT | Duration: ~58m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Rajiv, Sara, Tom (Atlas Financial)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Maya from Redwood, and with me is Diego our systems SE. How's it going?
[00:08] Rajiv: Morning, thanks for squeezing us in. We got a couple people pulled in, I'm Rajiv, head of ML at Atlas. Sara's on for platform stuff and Tom is here for overall architecture.
[00:15] Maya: Awesome, quick agenda — we'll do a short Optimize walkthrough focusing on batching and prefix / KV cache recommendations, go over a cost model and then outline a benchmark plan. Any other must-haves?
[00:25] Tom: We'd like to confirm latency SLOs and the privacy story — VPC, KMS, and audit logs are top of mind.
[00:32] Maya: Totally, we'll hit that.

[02:05] Diego: To start, quick question on profile — what is your current traffic shape? Are you doing low-latency interactive queries for trading alerts or more batch-reporting?
[02:15] Rajiv: It's primarily interactive — trader-facing suggestions, under 200ms P50 desired, P95 under 500ms ideally, and about 300 reqs/sec during spikes. We also have nightly batch runs but those are less sensitive.
[02:30] Sara: Also, retention constraints — logs must be retained for 13 months and keys live in our on-prem HSM.

[04:00] Diego: Great. So on Optimize the two levers we almost always push first are batching policy and prefix/KV cache. Batching reduces amortized cost per token but can add a bit to latency depending on batch windows and the batching algorithm (dynamic vs fixed).
[04:20] Maya: The other piece is prefix or KV cache for repeated context — for your workload the trader prompts reuse a lot of prefix state (user profile, etc) so KV cache can cut compute substantially.

[06:10] Rajiv: Quick clarification — prefix vs KV cache, I sometimes see both used interchangeably in docs. What's the practical diff?
[06:20] Diego: Good question; prefix caching is basically caching entire prompt prefixes or encoded KV pairs for common prefixes. KV cache is the runtime's internal key-value attention cache reused across tokens to avoid recomputing past context. For Redwood's Optimize we expose both: short-term prefix cache for deterministic prefixes (like system prompts) and the runtime KV cache reuse across sessions. Practically, prefix cache helps for cold-start of common prompts; KV cache matters for long-running streams or sessions.

[08:40] Sara: How much cost savings can we expect?
[08:45] Diego: Depends on hit rate. In our model, a 60% prefix hit rate plus KV reuse on 30% of tokens can reduce GPU compute token ops by up to 45% for typical chat-style workloads. We'll share the spreadsheet but ballpark we saw cost/unit go from $0.012/token to about $0.0065/token with aggressive caching and batching on a 4k model.

[10:10] Tom: Those per-token numbers are helpful. I assume there's a CPU/network overhead with caching?
[10:17] Diego: Yes small overhead — prefix cache lookups and KV cache lookups are very cheap compared to recomputing attention, but network egress for distributed caches and serialization can add microseconds. This is where placement matters: colocating cache with inference instances reduces tail latency.

[12:00] Rajiv: Can you run through a simple cost math example?
[12:10] Maya: Sure — say baseline hosted inference without batching is 1k tokens per request, average of 300k tokens per hour -> cost X. If you apply adaptive batching that increases GPU utilization and cuts per-token cost by ~30%, and prefix cache hit reduces tokens touched by 40% on average, combined you could see ~60% cost reduction in GPU compute spend. Diego, want to mention the spreadsheet link?
[12:35] Diego: Yes — we'll send 'benchmarks/atlas-batching-kv.xlsx' (link shared in chat). That has assumptions: model size, qps distribution, batch window ms, and cache hit rate scenarios.

[14:00] Sara: On latency, batching worries me; if we batch up to 50ms to improve utilization but we need 200ms P50 that's tight. How do you tune batching to avoid SLO misses?
[14:12] Diego: We recommend dynamic batching with a priority on latency SLOs — set per-route latency budgets. Redwood Optimize can set a max batch wait (e.g., 10ms for trader route) and then fall back to dedicated low-latency pool for critical routes. Also we support tail latency guarding and can route high-priority requests to smaller batch sizes or reserved capacity.

[16:20] Tom: This is where Dedicated might make sense — predictable throughput and lower jitter. But we also have compliance concerns that push us to Private. Any differences in caching/enabled features across modes?
[16:35] Maya: Functionally the runtime is consistent across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Differences are operational: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and stronger latency consistency; Private gives you VPC and on-prem integration for keys and logs. Cache colocations are available in Dedicated and Private for tighter latency; hosted can also do region-specific cache nodes but we may need to talk about placement.

[18:10] Rajiv: About keys — we need KMS/HSM integration with our on-prem HSM. Is that supported?
[18:18] Diego: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM. For Dedicated we can do a VPC peering and KMS integration; for Hosted we offer envelope encryption but not direct HSM pinning. We'll share our KMS integration notes.

[20:00] Maya: Quick demo slide — here's an example config: route-level batching allowed {max_batch_size: 64, max_wait_ms: 15}, prefix_cache_ttl: 1hr, kv_cache_eviction: lru, kv_cache_size: 8GB.
[20:20] Rajiv: How do evictions affect correctness? If we evict mid-session will model behavior change?
[20:30] Diego: If KV entries are evicted you'll lose cache hits and recompute the past context, so semantics remain the same; it only impacts cost and latency, not correctness. For session continuity we often keep hot sessions pinned to cache if needed.

[22:10] Sara: For our nightly batches we could use different config?
[22:15] Maya: Exactly — per-route policies let you have aggressive batching for nightly jobs and low-latency configs for trader endpoints.

[24:00] Diego: Now a practical run-through on the cost model: we model per-token compute cost, memory footprint for kv cache, and network overhead for cache hits. For example scenario A (no caching, conservative batching) costs $14k/month; scenario B (prefix + KV with 50% hit, medium batching) costs $6k/month; scenario C (dedicated with colocated cache) costs $7.5k/month but with better P95. Numbers in spreadsheet reflect instance pricing assumptions.

[26:40] Rajiv: How accurate are these estimates for our infra? We run on-prem HSM and have tight egress controls, some variance expected.
[26:50] Diego: Estimates rely on your sample traces — that's why the benchmark run with your traffic is key. We'll run an apples-to-apples benchmark using your anonymized traces and our runtime. Expect some delta but usually within 10-20% of model.

[29:00] Tom: Could we do an A/B: route 1 on hosted with caching, route 2 on dedicated, compare cost & latency?
[29:10] Maya: Yes, we often do split routing for pilots; Redwood supports routing by policy so you can direct production traffic incrementally.

[31:20] Rajiv: Any gotchas for multi-tenant caching and security? If we colocate caches, how do we ensure tenant isolation?
[31:30] Diego: We isolate cache namespaces by tenant and enforce encryption at rest for cache backing stores. For Private deployments you can hold cache backing store inside your VPC. We'll share the security doc snippet.

[33:10] Sara: About observability — can we get token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route?
[33:18] Maya: Yes Redwood Console gives token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, and trace links. We can also export to your datadog or prometheus.

[34:40] Rajiv: For benchmarking, what's the format you need for traces?
[34:50] Diego: An NDJSON with timestamp, request tokens, model type, and route label works. The spreadsheet has a sample script.

[36:00] (crosstalk)
[36:12] Rajiv: Ok we'll prep a 7-day sample.

[38:20] Diego: One more thing on batching heuristics — we support dynamic batching that adapts to QPS shape; for bursty spikes you get fast fill but we still keep tail latency guard rails. TTLs and batch windows are the knobs.

[40:00] Tom: If we go Dedicated, how long to provision?
[40:06] Maya: Typically 2-4 weeks for initial reserved capacity depending on region and GPU type. Private on-prem will take longer due to networking and KMS integration.

[42:30] Rajiv: Any compliance paperwork we need? SOC2, ISO, and a data processing addendum.
[42:38] Maya: We'll send SOC2 and ISO artifacts; we also have a DPA template and can work with your legal team.

[44:10] Sara: Are there limits to cache sizes? We have a lot of user profiles — could we face memory pressure?
[44:18] Diego: Cache sizes are configurable; you can set per-tenant budgets and ring-fence. Also we can tier cold objects to SSD-backed stores if needed, at higher latency.

[46:00] Maya: Recap: 1) We'll run SE-led benchmarks using your 7-day trace. 2) We'll share pricing & security docs. 3) We'll propose a pilot window and routing plan.

[47:20] Rajiv: Sounds good. A couple of specific asks — please include a breakdown that isolates GPU cost vs infra/ops cost and a sensitivity analysis on cache hit rate.
[47:35] Diego: We'll include that in the spreadsheet — sensitivity tables for hit rate 0-90% and different batch windows.

[49:10] Tom: On the pilot, we care about rollback and safety — if latency regresses we need automatic fallback to smaller models or alternate region.
[49:20] Maya: Redwood supports automatic fallbacks and can route to a simpler model variant or to a dedicated cold standby. We can configure canary rollouts and automatic rollbacks.

[51:00] Rajiv: Any notes about model quantization tradeoffs? We care about quality for trader prompts.
[51:10] Diego: Quantization can reduce cost but might affect generation quality slightly; we recommend running quality regressions on a held-out eval set. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles by workload and will flag regressions.

[53:20] Sara: For the benchmark, can you also run a tail-latency focused test rather than just averages?
[53:28] Diego: Absolutely, we'll include P50/P90/P95/P99 in the report.

[55:00] Maya: Any final questions?
[55:05] Rajiv: No, just timeline — we'll aim to get traces to Diego by 2026-07-18 and expect the benchmark week of 2026-07-20.

[55:15] Maya: Perfect. We'll follow up with calendar invite and the artifact links — SOC2 pack, benchmark spreadsheet (drive/benchmarks/atlas-batching-kv.xlsx), and the sample trace script.

[55:30] Tom: Thanks everyone.

[55:33] Maya: Thanks all, talk soon.

[57:00] End of meeting.
